extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians and mathematical physicists, and historians/philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing mathematical and physicists' methods—when heuristic/speculative techniques are acceptable, and how such practices can be assimilated into rigorous mathematics. Focuses on proof standards, reinterpretation strategies, and success conditions for giving dubious techniques a formal foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conjecture/speculation from rigorous results
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of distinguishing between conjecture and mathematical speculation; separating results based on rigorous proofs from those which have a heuristic basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jaffe and Quinn warn that failure to distinguish conjecture from speculation can drop the reliability of the literature and create unfair reward distributions. Atiyah and Thurston stress 'the importance of distinguishing between results based on rigorous proofs and those which have a heuristic basis' (Atiyah et al., 1994).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof must convey conviction (community-dependent standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is something that conveys conviction that a given assertion is true; what counts as a proof can vary between mathematicians and physicists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes there is no single notion of proof in physics (ranging from fully rigorous proofs to formal manipulations backed by simulations), whereas mathematics has a more standardized notion; X. G. Viennot's remark about treating experimental formulae as 'experimentally true' but 'mathematically ... just a conjecture' exemplifies differing community standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-theoretic foundations and precise definitions for rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorous mathematical argument requires that objects be defined as set-theoretical objects (e.g., on the basis of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory) with fundamental properties established from axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter describes 20th-century mathematics' consensus on set-theoretical foundations, giving contemporary mathematics unity and cohesion; alternative foundations (e.g., category theory) are reconcilable via general techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/numerical agreement as pragmatic acceptance in physics
rubrics_metrics.description: When computations agree with experiment or extensive numerical evidence, physicists may consider formulas 'experimentally true' even if mathematically unproved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viennot: when many known elements of a sequence allow a guessed formula with infinitesimal probability of being wrong, it can be treated as experimentally true. The text cites examples such as Feynman diagram computations agreeing to many decimal places producing physicists' trust despite lack of full mathematical formulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success criterion for assimilation: provide consistent conceptual framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory assimilation of speculative/heuristic methods must provide a consistent conceptual framework in which previously puzzling computations make sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For historical and contemporary anomalous techniques, the rules of success are 'to provide a consistent conceptual framework in which the puzzling computations make sense.' This is the ‘criteria of success’ for reinterpretation of older methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinterpretation must reproduce important calculations and concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: A rigorous interpretation should at minimum reproduce some of the most important calculations and concepts of the older (dubious) technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that no interpretation can be perfect in every respect, but 'the most we can ask is that a rigorous interpretation reproduce at least some of the most important calculations and concepts of the older technique.' Examples: Robinson's nonstandard analysis reproducing many Leibnizian procedures; Rota's interpretation of umbral calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear semantics for previously tacit operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every step of formerly informal manipulations semantically clear (e.g., by introducing operators, linear functionals, or formal power series to explain symbolic moves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Blissard's raising/lowering of indices in the umbral calculus is given semantics by interpreting representative variables as coefficients via a linear functional L on the polynomial algebra, so each step can be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction of higher-type objects as legitimate reinterpreting strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of higher-type entities (e.g., linear functionals, ultrapowers/hyperreals, probability measures) to give semantics to anomalous objects is an acceptable strategy for assimilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rota's linear operator L, Robinson's ultrapower construction for hyperreals, and the representation of quantum mechanical entities as probability measures are cited as ways higher types explain and legitimize previously dubious operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to revise logical foundations when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Change in logical basis (for example, abandoning classical logic) can be an acceptable move if it yields a consistent theory that models the informal practice (e.g., smooth infinitesimal analysis uses intuitionistic logic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter discusses smooth infinitesimal analysis where all functions are continuous and microlinearity holds, at the price of non-classical logic; Quine's view that no part of science is immune from revision is invoked to justify such changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation should be heuristically fertile and connect to broader theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A good reinterpretation not only legitimizes previous computations but also bears fruit—connecting to wider mathematics and enabling systematic treatments of related concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rota's embedding of the umbral calculus in formal power series and linear algebra is cited as producing fertile connections (special functions, category theory, adjoints) beyond merely legitimizing Blissard's manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat impossibility theorems as guides to alternative interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Impossibility theorems that rule out obvious interpretations do not preclude all rigorous formulations; they indicate that alternative frameworks should be sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Berkeley's criticism is evaded by changing logic; Cameron's result about no Feynman measure rules out certain obvious measures but doesn't forbid other ways to make sense of Feynman integrals. The text encourages optimism in finding alternate rigorous meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify work by degree of rigour but recognize productive fringe practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a distinction between fully rigorous work and broadly mathematical but non-rigorous work, while recognizing that engineers and physicists' calculational traditions can be productive and deserve attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay takes for granted 'a more or less clear distinction to be made between fully rigorous work, and work that is lacking rigour, even though it may be broadly mathematical in some sense.' It stresses studying how speculative parts are incorporated into rigorous research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/interpretive success measured by making old computations intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: In historical exegesis, success is judged by providing interpretations that give consistent meaning to puzzling or apparently contradictory computations from past practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter contrasts philosophical exegesis (less clear rules) with historical mathematics, where the criteria of success for interpreting older computations are 'fairly simple—to provide a consistent conceptual framework in which the puzzling computations make sense.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization of anomalous objects (e.g., Dirac delta) as acceptance criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: An anomalous object should be captured by an appropriate formal mathematical notion (e.g., distributions for the Dirac delta) that preserves intended properties while fitting into rigorous theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses the Dirac delta function as an example of a mathematically non-existent naive object; rigorous treatment requires new formalization (implied: theory of distributions) to recover its properties without contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for exploratory 'buccaneering' methods early in development with later standards enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowance for exploratory, speculative, or 'buccaneering' methods in early development stages may be justified, provided that later the community separates heuristic from proven results and enforces standards of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atiyah's remark advocates exploration of new ideas 'in their creative phase' though not a wholesale weakening of standards—Mac Lane counters by warning against piracy; the chapter highlights a nuanced position allowing early-stage freedom with later rigorous clarification.
